chunks: What limits switching frequency. The question: What limits the switching frequency?
A switching drive is limited by whichever of several things runs out first.
The main limit is heat: each switching transition wastes a little energy, so losses grow in step with frequency.
Fixed delays, like dead time and the minimum pulse width, eat a bigger share of each shorter period.
The circuit that drives the switch, the timer, and electrical noise (EMI) also set ceilings.
There is a lower limit too, because slow switching gives large ripple and audible whine.
Think of stirring a pot of soup. Stir faster and the soup stays smoother, which is lower ripple, but your arm tires faster, which is heat.
Each stroke also has fixed pauses at each end while you reverse. When the strokes are long, the pauses barely matter.
When you stir very fast, the pauses become most of each stroke.
Conduction loss is constant, switching losses grow linearly with frequency (on a log axis the curve bends upward). With a 1.
3 watts thermal budget (horizontal line: ΔT = 65 degrees Celsius at 50 degrees Celsius/W) the ceiling is near 257 kilohertz for this FET and edge speed.
Shortening the edges or lowering the voltage moves the ceiling up ("Increasing the switching frequency"). The model ignores the rise of R DS(on) with temperature.

Drag the edge time up to 300 nanoseconds and the ceiling falls to about 95 kilohertz; drag the conduction loss up to 1 watts instead and it falls to about 86 kilohertz, because less of the budget is left for switching.
Switching loss: energy wasted each time the switch changes state, because for a moment it carries current and voltage at once.
Dead time: a deliberate gap where both switches of a pair are off, so they never overlap. Minimum on-time: the shortest pulse the circuit can reliably make.
Current ripple: the wiggle in motor current from switching on and off. Faster switching shrinks it. Thermal budget: how much heat the part can shed without getting too hot.
A 12 volts, 5 amps drive whose switch spends 100 nanoseconds per cycle changing state, and has 16 milliohms of resistance when hot, loses about 0.
47 watts at 20 kilohertz, and about 2. 15 watts at 500 kilohertz. With a 1. 3 watts thermal budget, the ceiling is near 250 kilohertz.
Fixed times bite sooner: 200 nanoseconds of dead time on each of two edges is 0. 8% of a 20 kilohertz period, but 40% of a 1 megahertz period. That is the whole idea.
"Mainly loss and timing.
Switching loss, half V I times rise-plus-fall time times f, plus gate-drive, C oss and diode recovery losses, all scale with frequency and add to conduction loss until the thermal limit.
Then dead time, minimum on-time and blanking eat a bigger share of a shorter period, gate drivers can only supply so much current, and the timer resolution caps the frequency.
EMI rises too. The lower bound is ripple and audible noise, so motors typically run 20 to 50 kilohertz."
